statements.heading: Problem FoL.1 . . . librarian’s problem
statements.text:
A stack of 40 books lies on the ground. Each of them is d = 2 cm thick and has mass m = 1 kg.
We want to place the books into 4 shelves, with each shelf containing a stack of 10 books lying
on the side and the shelves’ are at heights 100 cm, 130 cm, 160 cm a 190 cm. What work do we
have to perform to move the books?

statements.heading: Problem FoL.2 . . . tough slice of bread
statements.text:
A square wheat field covers an area of 16 ha. A harvesting company owns a combine harvester
whose reel is 8 m wide. The combine moves with velocity 5 km·h−1 and it consumes 10 litres of
fuel per kilometer when harvesting. The company buys the fuel for 28.40 CZK per litre. How
much will harvesting the whole field cost the company (rounded to integer CZK), if they have
to pay the combine driver 85 CZK for each started hour of work? Neglect any delays of the
combine due to turning or fires in the field.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.3 . . . curve
statements.text:
Olda is driving a car with velocity v = 20 m·s−1; he keeps an air freshener on his rear view
mirror. When crossing a curve, his air frshener tilted by α = 35◦. What’s the radius of the
curve Olda was crossing? The acceleration due to gravity is g = 9.81 m·s−2.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.4 . . . astral
statements.text:
Dr Strange is an impenitent pragmatist who does not believe in out-of-body experiences. A nun
wants to correct his mistake by hitting him in the chest with a constant force and knocking the
astral body (with mass identical to that of Dr Strange, m = 80 kg) out of him. If the impact
(contact of the fist and the chest) took t = 0.1 s and the astral body was moving with velocity
v = 5 m·s−1 afterwards, what force did the nun hit with? The body of Dr Strange itself does
not move, violation of mass conservation is not our problem.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.5 . . . don’t mind the tune
statements.text:
Meggy brought a flute to a campfire. The flute is made of the ABS polymer with thermal
expansion coefficient α = 9 · 10−5 K−1. When she tried playing it indoors at 20 ◦C, its lowest
tone had frequency 349 Hz and the flute had length l. Near the fire, she placed the flute on
a bench. Assuming that the period of sound waves forming each tone is proportional to the
length of the flute, determine the frequency of its lowest tone, if the flute got heated up to 25 ◦C
in the meantime.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.6 . . . little cubes
statements.text:
Assume the molecules of water to be cubes in close contact (the volume of water is completely
filled by the cubes). Determine the number of molecules that fit in V ′ = 1 nm3 of volume.
Consider the water to be at standard conditions (T ≈300 K, p ≈1 atm), look up the necessary
values of water density, molar mass and Avogadro’s number (if you don’t know them by heart).

statements.heading: Problem FoL.7 . . . methane
statements.text:
At the bottom of, for example, the South China Sea, is a substance know as methane clathrate.
It’s a crystal of water ice with gaps in which methane molecules are enclosed. These gaps are
present in common ice as well, but they aren’t filled by any substance. The chemical formula of
this clathrate is CH4 · 5.75H2O. How many m3 of methane can be released to the atmosphere
at temperature 0 ◦C and pressure 100 kPa from 1 m3 of the clathrate? Water ice density is
917 kg·m−3.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.8 . . . do it tomorrow
statements.text:
Compute how long would day on Earth have to be in order to cause weightlessness at the
equator. The Earth’s radius is R = 6, 400 km, its mass is M = 6 · 1024 kg, the gravitational
constant is G = 6.7 · 10−11 kg−1·m3·s−2. Assume the Earth to be spherical.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.9 . . . Toricelli reloaded
statements.text:
We are on a space station with standard atmospheric pressure pa = 101 kPa inside, performing
the Toricelli experiment. We take a bottle of mercury, stick a long test tube inside and when it is
full, place it vertically in such a way that the open end is submerged under the surface of mercury
in the bottle. During the experiment, the space station is sufficiently far from the gravitational
influence of any celestial bodies and is accelerating in the direction of the closed end of the test
tube (after the above described manipulation) with acceleration a = 20 m·s−2. How high will
the mercury column in the test tube be? The density of mercury is ϱ = 13 600 kg·m−3.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.10 . . . effectiveness evaluation
statements.text:
Karel and Aleš have one homogeneous brick each. The bricks have cuboid shapes with edge
lengths a × a × 2a, where a = 5 cm. The mass of each brick is m = 1 kg. Karel puts his brick
down and starts flipping it in one direction always about the shorter edge (looking from the
side, the longer edge and the shorter edge alternate in touching the ground), until the brick
crosses a distance d = 150 cm. Aleš is also flipping his brick until it crosses the distance d, but
he is flipping it about the longer edges only (only the square base of the cuboid is ever visible
from the side). The bricks do not slip and collisions with the ground are inelastic. How much
more work will Karel perform? The acceleration due to gravity is g = 9.81 m·s−2.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.11 . . . ’murican
statements.text:
Náry does not like unpleasant surprises. How far from the muzzle of an air gun does he have
to stand in order to hear the shot exactly one second before he would get hit? The speed of
sound is 334 m·s−1, the exit velocity of the bullet is 152 m·s−1, the elevation angle of the shot
is 10◦. Neglect air resistance. The term ”heard” is considered equivalent to Náry being reached
by the sound wave. The time the bullet spends inside the muzzle is also negligible. Compute
the answer to metre precision.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.12 . . . from Prague to Brno
statements.text:
You are driving from Prague to Brno with velocity v = 150 km·h−1 on the D1 motorway. The
length of this path is d = 196 km. How many times will you pass by a RegioJet bus (also heading
to Brno) during driving, if you know that every half hour, a bus leaves Prague for Brno with
velocity vb = 80 km·h−1 and you leave Prague at the same time as one bus? (Don’t count that
bus, However, if you meet a bus when arriving at Brno, do count that one.) Assume that there
are no traffic jams or closed sections of the motorway due to construction.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.13 . . . and the Sun in Ophiuchus means that. . .
statements.text:
What is the maximum force that Jupiter can exert on a FYKOS member on Earth? The FYKOS
member has mass mF = 85.6 kg, look up the remaining parameters. Assume that the orbits
of Jupiter and Earth are circular with radii equal to the lengths of their semi-major axes and
coplanar.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.14 . . . bounce from zero
statements.text:
In the xy plane, there is a perfectly reflecting mirror represented by the curve x2 + y2 = 1,
y < 0. We send a light ray towards the concave side of the mirror along the line x =
√
3/2.
How many times will the ray reflect before flying back to the half-plane y > 0?

statements.heading: Problem FoL.15 . . . St. Elmo’s sphere
statements.text:
What’s the minimum radius r of a conducting sphere such that there’s no spontaneous discharge,
if the charge of the sphere is Q = 1 C? In air, spontaneous discharge occurs if the electric field
reaches Emax = 25 kV·cm−1.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.16 . . . under pressure
statements.text:
We put a metal rod of length l = 1 m into a hydraulic press. The ends of the rod are held in
a way that creates a small stress σ0. The rod’s thermal expansion coefficient is α = 1.1·10−5 K−1
and its Young modulus is E = 200 GPa. We heat up the rod by ∆T = 1 K. Calculate the change
in stress in the rod if the rams of the press do not move and are not thermally conducting.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.17 . . . long drop
statements.text:
We throw a polystyrene ball of radius r = 1.0 cm and density ϱ = 0.06 g·cm−3 vertically down
into a ventillation shaft. In the shaft, hot warm air with density ϱa = 1.1 kg·m−3 flows up with
velocity v0 = 10 m·s−1. Determine the magnitude of terminal velocity of the ball with respect
to the shaft, if the drag coefficient of the ball is C = 0.50 and the acceleration due to gravity
is g = 9.8 m·s−2.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.18 . . . microrotation
statements.text:
The molar mass of water is M = 18 g·mol−1. Its molecules have a certain rotational energy
with characteristic scale ε = 650 J·mol−1. The linear dimension of one molecule (its diameter)
is l = 310 pm. Using dimensional analysis, determine the characteristic scale for the period of
rotation. The answer is the base-10 logarithm of this period in seconds.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.19 . . . perfectly balanced
statements.text:
Consider a thin homogeneous disk of radius r, supported in the middle. Initially, there were
two point masses m placed on the perimeter of the disk opposite each other so that the system
remained balanced. We want to replace one of the masses by a pair of masses 3m/5 and 4m/5,
both placed on the perimeter of the disk, so that the system still remained balanced. How far
(in multiples of r) from each other do the two replacement masses have to be?

statements.heading: Problem FoL.21 . . . chain reaction
statements.text:
We placed a large number of balls of radius r = 1 cm in a line. The distance of centers of any
two successive balls is d = 5 cm. Each ball has mass m = 20 g and rolling friction coefficient
ξ = 0.6 mm. The first ball in the line is given a velocity v = 1 m·s−1 in order to start a series
of central collisions of the balls. Which ball will be the last one to move? All collisions are
perfectly elastic and the balls don’t slip. The acceleration due to gravity is g = 9.81 m·s−2.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.22 . . . ready steady
statements.text:
We placed two identically charged particles with masses m = 1 g and charges q = 1 μC at
a height h = 2 m above the ground. Afterwards, we release them and measure the velocity of
one of the particles just before colliding wiťh the ground to be v = 10 m·s−1. How much did the
electrostatic potential energy decrease between the start of the movement and this moment?
The acceleration due to gravity is g = 9.81 m·s−2.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.23 . . . it hangs – it hangs
statements.text:
In a laboratory, a polystyrene ball of mass m1 = 1 kg and density ϱ = 1 020 kg·m−3 hangs on
a massless rope. The molar heat capacity of polystyrene is c = 1 400 J·kg−1·K−1, its thermal
expansion coefficient is α = 7 · 10−5 K−1. On another rope, we hang another ball made of the
same material and with mass m2 = 0.5 kg. To each ball, we transfer heat Q = 5 kJ, which
increases the energy of the first ball by E1 and of the second ball by E2. Find the difference
E2 −E1. The acceleration due to gravity is g = 9.81 m·s−2.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.24 . . . eccentric travelling companion
statements.text:
Given the ratio of velocities of a planet on an eliptical trajectory around a star in the pericenter
(the point of the trajectory closest to the star) and in the apocenter (the point farthest from
the star) vp/va = K =
√
2, what’s the numerical (relative) eccentricity ε of that trajectory?

statements.heading: Problem FoL.26 . . . tuning
statements.text:
In the middle of a field, there’s Pepa with a tuning fork emitting a sound with frequency
f1 = 440 Hz. You’re driving away from Pepa with velocity v = 70 km·h−1. What will be the
frequency f of the sound you hear? The speed of sound in air is vs = 330 m·s−1.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.27 . . . aloha snackbar
statements.text:
The US President’s airplane has range approximately 12 600 km. Once upon a time, it was
hijacked by terrorists shortly after takeoff, with the president on board, and vanished from the
radars. A thorough search of both land and ocean was launched immediately. What area (in
km2) has to be searched if the terrorists can’t refuel anywhere?

statements.heading: Problem FoL.28 . . . burst
statements.text:
Into how many smaller droplets could a larger water droplet break, if it fell from a h = 50 cm
height? Consider all droplets to be spherical. The radius of the original droplet is r = 1 cm
(with its center of mass at height h) and the droplets it breaks into should have equal sizes.
The surface tension of water is σ = 73 mN·m−1 and its density is ϱ = 1.00 g·cm−3. We’re only
looking for an estimate of an upper bound of the number of droplets based on the energetic
balance at the beginning and at the end.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.29 . . . damped oscillation
statements.text:
There’s a mass point that oscillates along the y axis. The oscillation is described by the equa-
tion y = yme−bt sin(ωt + φ0), where ym is the initial amplitude, b = 0.05 s−1 is the damping
coefficient, ω = 200 Hz is the angular frequency and φ0 is the initial angular displacement.
When will the maximal amplitude decrease below ym/2?

statements.heading: Problem FoL.30 . . . don’t stick your fingers in!
statements.text:
A large ceiling fan may be approximated as a disk of radius r = 10 cm and mass M = 0.5 kg,
with three rods attached, pointing away from the centre of the disk. Each rod has length l =
= 40 cm and mass m = 0.2 kg. The fan rotates with frequency f = 1 Hz. What work do we
need to perform to stop the fan? All parts of the fan are homogeneous, neglect any friction.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.31 . . . dark planet
statements.text:
What’s the radius of a sphere with Earth-like density ϱ = 5.50 g·cm−3, but escape velocity
equal to the speed of light? We’re interested in the first-order approximation, i.e. neglecting
relativistic effects. Assume that the planet’s density is constant (the planet is homogeneous).
Give the result as a multiple of the radius of Earth RZ = 6, 371 km.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.32 . . . crash
statements.text:
The Moon is an approximately homogeneous sphere of mass M = 7.3 · 1022 kg and radius R =
= 1, 700 km, rotating with a period T = 27 d. A megameteorite of mass m = M/1 000 collides
with the Moon’s equator under an incidence angle ϑ = 45◦into the lunar soil, against the
direction of rotation. The impact velocity is v = 10 km·s−1. How long will the lunar day be
after the impact, if the debris from the meteorite spreads evenly over the surface of the Moon?
The meteorite and the Moon are both made of the same material. Neglect mutual gravitational
influence of the bodies before the impact. Give the result as a positive number in the units of
(Earth’s) days.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.33 . . . just a little closer
statements.text:
There are two hooks on two opposite walls with distance d = 1 m. On one hook, there’s a charge
q = 1 μC. On the other hook, there’s no charge, but a thin non-conducting massless rope of
length l = d, with a ball with mass m = 2 g and charge −q on its other end. Find the smallest
angle (in ◦) between the rope and the wall such that the ball is at rest.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.34 . . . chain reaction II
statements.text:
We placed a large number of identical ice cuboids with square bases of side a = 2 cm in a line
on an ice rink. The distance between centers of any two successive cuboids is d = 5 cm. Each
cuboid has mass m = 20 g and the friction coefficients (both static and dynamic) are f = 0.03.
The first cuboid in the line is given a velocity v0 = 1 m·s−1 in order to start a series of central
collisions of the cuboids. Which cuboid will be the last one to move? All collisions are perfectly
inelastic, the cuboids don’t tilt and are placed in such a way that they have parallel sides. The
acceleration due to gravity is g = 9.81 m·s−2.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.35 . . . Newton’s rings
statements.text:
Olda was watching Newton’s glass. Compute the distance of the 2nd minimum of the interference
circles from the center, if we know that the light incident on it has wavelength λ = 500 nm,
the refraction index of glass is ns = 1.5 and the refraction index of air is nv = 1. The radius of
curvature of the upper glass is r = 20 cm.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.36 . . . short circuit
statements.text:
There’s a simple electric circuit with two elements: a DC source with voltage U = 1 V and
internal resistance R = 1 Ω, and a coil with N = 200 turns of copper winding (circular cross-
section), length l = 30 cm, inner radius r1 = 1.90 cm and outer radius r2 = 2.05 cm. What’s the
maximum current passing through the coil after we switch on the source? The temperature in
the room is 20 ◦C, neglect any heating of the winding.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.37 . . . exoplanet
statements.text:
An exoplanet of radius rp = 8.0·103 km is in circular orbit around a distant star with mass M =
= 1.0 · 1030 kg. The orbit and the observer are coplanar. A transit of the planet across the star
was observed. The time from the first decrease in brightness until brightness returned to its
initial value was T = 2.0 hours and the maximum decrease in brightness was 0.3 %. Determine
the orbital radius.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.38 . . . tse-tse
statements.text:
Little rabbit has a prescription for sleeping pills. When he takes 1/3 of a pill, he sleeps for 5
hours. When he takes 2/3 of a pill, he sleeps for 9 hours. Once, little rabbit went nuts and
took 100 pills. How many hours did he sleep, if we know that little rabbit sleeps only when the
medicine’s concentration in blood exceeds a certain value? Assume that the rate at which the
medicine is broken down is proportional to its concentration. Neglect any medicine left over in
blood from the previous days or little rabbit’s death.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.39 . . . throwing peas at the wall
statements.text:
Mirek was sitting on an office chair with wheels at work, looking at a wall deep in thoughts.
In order to do something more useful, he took a sack of peas and started throwing them at
a wall. There are n = 3, 600 peas in the sack, each of them weighs mh = 0.2 g and Mirek is
throwing them with a frequency f = 0.5 s−1. The peas are thrown horizontally with velocity
vh = 10 m·s−1. What will Mirek’s velocity be after emptying the sack? The mass of Mirek +
chair is mM = 60 kg, the chair moves without friction.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.40 . . . wire
statements.text:
There’s a thin, perfectly black wire with circular cross-section of radius r = 0.3 mm in thermal
equilibrium at room temperature (T0 = 20 ◦C) in vacuum. Under these conditions, the resistance
of the wire per unit length is R0 = 5 Ω/m. If the thermal coefficient of resistance is α =
= 0.004 K−1, determine the current that must pass through the wire so that its temperature
stabilised at 220 ◦C.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.41 . . . hydrophobe
statements.text:
There’s a water droplet on the horizontal part of an umbrella. The contact angle between the
droplet and the umbrella is quite large, ϑc = 120◦. The surface tension between water and air
is σlg = 73 mN·m−1. We add a bit of detergent to the droplet, decreasing the surface tension
to σ′
lg = 56 mN·m−1 and the contact angle to ϑ′
c = 90◦. How much did the surface tension
between the surface of the umbrella and the liquid have to change? Compute the result in units
mN·m−1!

statements.heading: Problem FoL.43 . . . merry-go-round
statements.text:
There’s a box of mass m = 5 kg and negligible size standing on a merry-go-round. The box
is r = 10 m far from the center of the merry-go-round; the static friction coefficient between
them is f0 = 1. The merry-go-round starts rotating from rest with linearly increasing angular
acceleration ε = kt, where k = 1 s−3. How long since the start of the rotation will it take for the
box to fly away from its initial position?

statements.heading: Problem FoL.44 . . . twin paradox
statements.text:
One of two twins leaves in a rocket for a planet s = 5 ly far from the Earth, while the other twin
stays at their home planet. The rocket moves with velocity v = 0.2c. At half the distance s, the
cosmonaut twin enters a fast module, which starts moving with respect to the original rocket
with velocity u = 0.1c towards the original goal of the rocket. How many years younger will
the cosmonaut twin be compared to the twin at the home planet? Neglect any effects caused
by acceleration or deceleration of the space vessels (as if they only passed by each other and
gravity did not exist). In order to avoid trouble with relativity of simultaneity, compare the
times spent by each twin waiting for the arrival of the fast module at the goal.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.46 . . . focus
statements.text:
On one side of a thin biconvex lens with identical radii of curvature R = 20 cm is a spherical
mirror placed coaxially in such a way that a ray that passes through the lens is reflected back
towards the lens. What is the (positive) focal length of such a system? The refractive index of
glass is n = 1.5.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.47 . . . Sisyphean labour
statements.text:
Sisyphos is standing at the bottom of a hemispherical hole of radius R = 100 m. His task is to
push an approximately spherical, bumpy rock of mass M = 1 000 kg and radius r = 50 cm. The
effective rolling friction coefficient of the rock is ξ = 4 cm. Sisyphos is pushing the rock up with
negligible constant velocity while exerting a force Fs, horizontally towards the center of mass of
the rock. Sisyphos runs out of stamina after performing work Ws = 200 kJ. By how much will
he lift the center of mass of the rock before it happens? Neglect changes in potential energy of
Sisyphos, the acceleration due to gravity is g = 9.81 m·s−2.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.48 . . . spin it
statements.text:
There is a bicycle on a bicycle stand. We know that its rear wheel’s moment of inertia around
its axis is I = 0.5 kg·m2 and its radius is r = 30 cm. We speed up the wheel by repeatedly
hitting it with a hand tangentially on its circumference in the direction of its rotation. The
speed of each hit in the rest reference frame is w = 5 m·s−1, the mass of the hand is m = 1.5 kg,
the hand loses all its velocity in the reference frame of the point of impact after the impact
(the hand is moving around an elbow, but we neglect rotation of the forearm). What will the
velocity of a point on the perimeter of the wheel after 10 hits be?

statements.heading: Problem FoL.49 . . . all day long
statements.text:
Imagine that the observable universe is spherical with diameter d = 1027 m and filled with stars
placed in the lattice points of a cubic grid with side length of the unit cell a = 1019 m. The stars
are identical and their radiation is isotropic with luminosity L = 1027 W and radius r = 109 m.
The stars don’t block other stars’ light; there is no absorption. What’s the incident power per
square metre near the centre of the universe in the middle of a body diagonal of a unit cell?
Compute the base-10 logarithm of this value!

statements.heading: Problem FoL.50 . . . comfy by the pond
statements.text:
It’s summer and we’re resting on a bank of a deep pond. The sun is shining, the acceleration due
to gravity is g = 9.81 m·s−2, the surface tension of water is σ = 72.8 mN·m−1, water density is
ϱ = 1 000 kg·m−3. At a distance d = 30.0 m from the bank, a backswimmer appears and creates
circular waves on the surface. When we focus on one wave, we can see that it’s moving with
speed c = 1.00 m·s−1. How long will it take for the wavefront of the backswimmer’s waves to
reach the bank? You may use the formula for phase velocity of deep-water waves c =

statements.heading: Problem FoL.51 . . . toast
statements.text:
We’d like to make a toast using a very strange glass. It’s a hollow cube of inner volume V = 1 l,
which is standing on one corner (a body diagonal is vertical). Through a small opening near
the top vertex, we fill the cube with V ′ = 1/3 l of wine. How high above the ground (i.e. the
vertex the cube is standing on) will the wine surface be? Neglect the thickness of the cube’s
sides. Compute the result as a multiple of the cube’s edge length!

statements.heading: Problem FoL.53 . . . you shall not transmit!
statements.text:
Consider a simple model of a static one-dimensional atmosphere, denoting its relevant coordi-
nate (elevation) by h. If we took a thin slice of this atmosphere with thickness ∆h, its reflectance
would be r(h)∆h. What fraction of incident light is transmitted by the atmosphere if r(h) =
= r0e−kh, where k = r0 = 0.1 m−1?

statements.heading: Problem FoL.54 . . . transit
statements.text:
Consider a system in which infinitely many discrete states exist, indexed by an index i ∈N
(positive integers). The state of the whole system can be described by a state vector f =
= (f1, f2, . . . ), where fi denotes the number of objects in state i. The time evolution of the
system occurs in discrete steps. The probability of transition of an object from a state i to
the state i + 1 in one step is Pi,i+1 = 1/i2, the probability of transition from a state i to the
state i −1 is Pi,i−1 = 1 −Pi,i+1. It follows from basic properties of probability that transitions
between non-adjacent states or remaining in the same state isn’t allowed. Initially, all objects
are in state f1. Find the stationary state the system converges to and compute the number of
objects in the first state as a multiple of the total number of objects in the system N. Assume
that N is a very large number. The total number of objects remains constant during the time
evolution.

statements.heading: Problem FoL.55 . . . megamagnet
statements.text:
There’s a cylindrical coil of length l = 100 km and base diameter d = 1 km with N = 106
turns. There’s a current I = 1 kA passing through the coil. Determine the electric field felt
when flying out of the coil parallel to its axis at a distance r = 1 m from that axis with velocity
v = 1, 000 km·s−1. Neglect any effects of general relativity.

We have built a tower from three identical blocks with edge lengths a, b. Find the

statements.heading: Problem M.3 . . . collision imminent
statements.text:
Calculate the lowest possible energy loss resulting from a perfectly inelastic central collision of
two rigid balls with masses m = 3 kg and M = 2 kg. The speeds before the collision are 5 m·s−1
and 6 m·s−1 (with respect to a static observer).

statements.heading: Problem M.4 . . . stick like no other
statements.text:
Rigid homogeneous stick of length l = 1 m has been thrown upwards in a uniform gravitational
field. During its flight, there was a moment when the translational kinetic energy equaled the
rotational kinetic energy. We know that in that precise moment the speed of the stick’s center
of mass was 9 m·s−1. Find the instantaneous angular velocity of the stick upon its release.

statements.heading: Problem E.1 . . . charged Fykosák
statements.text:
Electrically neutral Fykos bird has been endowed with 1012 electrons. It then flies into a ho-
mogeneous electric field with speed v0 = 3.6 km·h−1 in a direction opposite to the direction
of the field lines. Electric intensity of the field is 500 V·m−1. What will be the speed v of the
Fykos bird after 100 m long flight in the electric field? Consider a point-like bird with mass m =
= 0.5 kg.

statements.heading: Problem E.2 . . . Náry’s hoverboard
statements.text:
How much current would have to flow through a horizontal wire 1 m long to make the wire
levitate above the ground? Magnetic induction is 5 · 10−5 T at the place where the wire is and
points to the north in the horizontal plane. The wire has a mass 50 g. The direction of the wire
is from west to east.

statements.heading: Problem E.3 . . . astonished Náry
statements.text:
Náry was playing with electrical components and ended up with four peculiar things. He was
told by others that they are a resistor with resistance R = 10 000 Ω, capacitor with capacity
C = 1 μF, inductor with inductance L = 10 H and alternating current source with voltage
U = 230 V and frequency f = 50 Hz. By some strange coincidence he managed to build a series
circuit. Knowing what he is playing with, he immediately computed the absolute value of phase
shift between current and voltage in the circuit. What number did he get?

statements.heading: Problem E.4 . . . it’s freezing
statements.text:
An arc lamp has resistivity 0.2 Ωand it is connected to voltage U = 60 V. How much heat does
it release during 1 min? Give the result in MJ.

statements.heading: Problem X.1 . . . Odysea and Prometheus
statements.text:
There are two space-ships, Odysea and Prometheus. Both of them have rest length L0 and both
are approaching the Earth, but from opposite direction. They meet in a point where Odysea
has speed 0.25c and Prometheus has speed 0.75c. How long do they appear to each other in
the moment when they pass each other? Determine the length as a multiple of L0.

statements.heading: Problem X.2 . . . who’s gonna survive
statements.text:
Let us have a beam of neutrons with kinetic energy T = 10 keV. Mean lifetime of a neutron is
τn = 925 s and its rest energy is mnc2 = 939.6 MeV. What percentage of neutrons in the beam
decays during passage through distance l = 10 m?

statements.heading: Problem X.3 . . . the winter, again
statements.text:
Consider a block of ice with mass mi = 5 kg and temperature ti = −2 ◦C. We place mFe = 3 kg
block of iron heated to tFe = 1 333 ◦C on the block of ice. Determine the resulting temperature
of the system. The specific heat capacity of ice is ci = 2.1 kJ·kg−1·K−1, the heat of fusion of ice
is lim = 334 kJ·kg−1, the specific heat capacity of water is cw = 4.18 kJ·kg−1·K−1, the latent
heat of evaporation of water is lvw = 2.26 MJ·kg−1 and the specific heat capacity of iron is
cFe = 473 J·kg−1·K−1

statements.heading: Problem X.4 . . . tiler
statements.text:
Are there such plane edge-to-edge tilings where, in every vertex, t equilateral triangles, s squares,
and h regular hexagons meet? We want to know how many such tilings exist. Numbers t, s, h
are non-negative integers. Sizes of polygons of the same type in one tiling are identical. The
arrangement of polygons about the vertex does not matter (different arrangements for fixed
s, t, h count as one).
